overview: Suriname’s history includes Indigenous and Maroon communities, colonial settlements and migration across oceans. Cooking tools, carved gifts, writing and family records offer different views of everyday knowledge. The examples identify particular places and communities.

periods.title: An English plantation colony
periods.summary: English colonisation under Francis Willoughby developed from 1650 and relied on enslaved labour. This colonial phase does not mark the beginning of Indigenous history.

periods.title: Dutch colonial government
periods.summary: Dutch forces captured the English colony in 1667 and regained it in 1668 after an English recapture. The Sociëteit van Suriname administered the colony from 1683 to 1795, followed by a new Dutch governing body.

periods.title: British occupation
periods.summary: Suriname came under British control in 1799. This first occupation ended in 1802.

periods.title: A brief return to Dutch government
periods.summary: Dutch administration resumed in 1802 before another British occupation in 1804.

periods.title: A second British occupation
periods.summary: Britain controlled the colony again from 1804. Transfer back to Dutch government took place in 1816, after the 1814 agreement.

periods.title: Dutch colonial rule and slavery
periods.summary: Dutch government resumed in 1816. Slavery remained legal until abolition in 1863.

periods.title: Abolition followed by compulsory labour
periods.summary: Slavery was abolished in 1863, but formerly enslaved people aged 15 to 60 had to enter labour agreements under state supervision. This system continued until 1873.

periods.title: Later colonial society and migration
periods.summary: State supervision ended in 1873. Indentured migration directly from British India continued from 1873 to 1916, forming one part of Suriname’s wider migration history.

periods.title: Internal autonomy within the Kingdom
periods.summary: The 1954 Charter made Suriname an autonomous country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Defence and foreign relations remained Kingdom responsibilities.

periods.title: The independent Republic of Suriname
periods.summary: Suriname became independent on November 25, 1975. This broad later period spans changing governments, including the military coup of 1980.

sections.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents

items.text: At Jodensavanne, excavations of House de Meza in 2020 to 2022 recovered pottery identified as Indigenous and Maroon alongside colonial objects. Work at a nearby cookhouse in 2023 and 2024 found Indigenous pottery in the same layer as colonial artifacts, plus a stone mortar. These finds support research into shared materials and cooking practices. They do not identify the maker or user of every pot, or prove equal relationships in a society shaped by slavery.

The Jodensavanne Foundation’s 2023 cookhouse record includes a nearly complete porcelain plate, part of a stoneware jug and an incomplete iron cauldron undergoing conservation. Different materials brought different qualities to serving, storing and cooking. Even fragments help reconstruct a working household. A recovered jug does not, by itself, reveal what someone drank from it on a particular day.

sections.title: Food tools with stories to tell

items.text: A basket sifter from Pikin Saron, a Kalina village, has a square wooden frame and loosely woven palm fibres. The Lam Museum’s 2022 account explains how such sifters remove lumps from cassava flour and make its texture more even. Weaving knowledge becomes useful kitchen equipment. Lumpy flour has met its match, without a plug or a battery in sight.

In 2018, visiting Matawai community members explained a decorated calabash spoon in the Smithsonian’s collection. They described this small spoon as a personal utensil for eating rice, with larger examples used for soup. Its bowl was cut from a hard-shelled gourd and decorated with incised designs. Community knowledge helps a museum understand how an object fits into meals and daily life.

A Ndyuka wooden food stirrer in Milwaukee’s collection carries carved personal messages. The museum describes carved utensils given as expressions of affection, with some stirrers used for cooking and more delicate examples kept for their beauty. A practical object can also hold a relationship’s meaning. The caption does not translate this particular message, so its exact words remain unstated here.

sections.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river

items.text: The Surinaams Museum preserves a mahogany four-poster bed made in 1829 by the furniture maker Podekowitz on Paramaribo’s Wagenwegstraat. It belongs to a collection rich in furniture associated with the colonial elite. This was substantial, carefully made furniture, rather than a picture of how everyone slept. A single grand bed cannot represent all the country’s bedrooms.

Needlework samplers in the same museum record how young European women practised embroidery and mending in the late nineteenth century. Surviving stitches make learning visible: someone had to repeat a movement, control the thread and improve. The collection also preserves early-twentieth-century baby clothes. These are particular surviving objects, rather than evidence that every family dressed or taught its children alike.

Gerrit Schouten’s 1817 miniature scene shows a riverboat with six enslaved rowers, a steersman and a covered passenger compartment. The shelter has windows with shutters propped open by sticks. The model records both ingenuity and inequality: passengers could travel out of the sun and rain while others did the rowing. It is an artist’s carefully constructed view, not a photograph of a named journey.

In the early twentieth century, Afáka Atumisi developed a writing system for Ndyuka. Its signs represent syllables. A 2012 study explains that the sign for tu, meaning two, uses two strokes, while fo, meaning four, uses four. A little counting can help a reading lesson. The system is a distinctive achievement in making spoken language visible, though some signs can represent more than one sound.

Immigration registers for indentured workers arriving from British India between 1873 and 1916 can record parents, siblings and other relatives. Officials later added marriages, children and sometimes grandchildren born in Suriname. These documents help descendants reconnect family stories across oceans. Some registers were lost or badly damaged, and spelling varies, so an unsuccessful name search does not show that a person never existed.

In September 2024, nineteen volunteers aged 12 to 70 joined a supervised archaeology project at Jodensavanne. Four young participants came from neighbouring Redi Doti, an Indigenous village. The work included excavation, maintenance and conservation; a caption records young volunteers sifting earth for artifacts. Learning about the past can involve patient observation and teamwork as well as books.

Jodensavanne’s heritage is cared for through cooperation with Redi Doti. UNESCO describes the Indigenous village and the Jodensavanne Foundation sharing responsibility for preservation and agreeing together on changes to the management plan. This recognises living communities as participants in caring for history. A historic site is also part of someone’s present-day neighbourhood.

ending.text: Suriname gained internal autonomy in 1954 and became an independent republic in 1975. These changes ended colonial government, not the histories of its communities. Crafts, languages and family knowledge continue through living people, with traditions changing as they are shared.
